title: The summit
hook: five years of stories, practices, texts, saints and silence, and the path goes on in eternity
tomorrow: what's the first step on the other side of the summit?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the greatest of these: love, the one that lasts and leaves nobody outside. The summit's lines, all together: I believe, I hope, I love; the portrait; you, by name; go, you are sent; hand it on; we praise thee, O God; in peace. Today, the top.
screen: `I BELIEVE · I HOPE · I LOVE.` → `THE PORTRAIT · YOU, BY NAME.` → `THE GREATEST OF THESE.`

segments.voice: Hikers will tell you the summit is a strange place. You take the photo, eat something, look at how small the parking lot is. And then, sooner than you'd like, you have to decide what's next, because nobody lives on a peak. So: you reach the top. Now what? The question is older than hiking. A psalm the Church prays puts it like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me." The mountain isn't the point. It's where you look up from.
screen: `THE PHOTO, THE SNACK, THE VIEW.` → `NOBODY LIVES ON A PEAK.` → `I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES.`

segments.voice: Look back down the mountain for a moment: stories, practices, the texts read in their own words, saints from every century, and a lot of silence. Paul has a word for what comes next, in the Douay-Rheims: "forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press towards the mark." Not forgetting as erasing; forgetting as not stopping. Gregory of Nyssa, an early Church Father, took the same idea further: for him, the one who seeks God never reaches an end to seeking, because God has no edge. And Paul again: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard," what God has prepared for those who love him. Catholics believe the path goes on past this life, into eternity. Now a neighbor. When a congregation finishes reading the Torah, Jewish tradition has them read the last lines of Deuteronomy and then, that same day, begin again: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." And at the end of each book, the room calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek: be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened. Shared ground: an ending that turns, right away, into a beginning. The honest difference: for Jews the circle of Torah begins again, here, together; for Catholics the summit points beyond this world, toward a God the eye hasn't seen. Two ways of not stopping. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: some traditions end their holy book by opening it again.
screen: `LOOK BACK DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` · `STRETCHING FORTH TO WHAT'S BEFORE.` · `NO EDGE TO GOD, NO END TO SEEKING.` · `THE LAST LINE, THEN IN THE BEGINNING.` · then, large: `THE SUMMIT IS A BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Stand up and stand still. Turn your head and look back over your shoulder, and name one thing from this whole climb you're thankful for. Then face forward and take a few slow steps, as if onto a new trail. If you pray, you can lift your eyes the way the psalm does, and say thank you.
The summit. Not the end of the path, but the place you look back, give thanks, and keep walking.
The last line to keep: the summit is a beginning, five years up and the path still going. Keep walking.

screen: `DAY 1791 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT'S THE FIRST STEP PAST THE SUMMIT?`

howItsDone: Catholics speak of the Christian life as a pilgrimage that continues into eternity; at the end of a retreat or a season of prayer, many simply begin the daily round of prayer again.

chat.meaning: The summit is a beginning: Paul keeps pressing on, and Jewish tradition turns the Torah's last line straight into In the beginning.

Gregory of Nyssa.meaning: an early Church Father and bishop who wrote on endless seeking

Torah.meaning: the five books of Moses, read through in the synagogue

Deuteronomy.meaning: the last book of the Torah

chazak, chazak, venitchazek.meaning: Hebrew: be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older English Catholic translation of the Bible
